paras: The Buckner mob hunt was an armed search for a Black man near Buckner, Missouri, on August 5, 1910, after Clara Baldus, a white farmer's daughter, was attacked in her home east of Independence. Wire reports said the mob threatened to burn the man if caught, but no report of a capture appears in the coverage. Fuller dispatches from Independence said the girl never saw her attacker, and the Black men questioned were released for lack of evidence.

Joseph Baldus, described as a Swiss farmer who owned 300 acres, lived on a farm nine miles east of Independence. On the morning of the attack he, his wife and their daughter Cora had driven to Kansas City to shop, leaving Clara, 16, alone to do the ironing.

According to her statement to deputy constable W. W. Twyman, Clara was lighting the gasoline stove when she heard footsteps, was seized by the throat, gagged with cotton and lost consciousness. She awoke nearly an hour later tied to a chair in the dining room, with the smell of chloroform in the air, freed herself and telephoned the Independence police. She said she was not hurt beyond the drug and the binding, and nothing was missing from the farm.

When the alarm spread, the neighborhood turned out, and a posse of about one hundred men, most from a nearby stone quarry, searched for the attacker. A Kansas City wire report described the searchers as a mob "armed with guns and clubs" hunting a "negro" in the brush near Buckner, accused of the attack, and said the mob threatened to burn him. The same report said another Black man had been "captured and spirited away by the authorities" and that two Black men were reported to have attacked the girl. The Grand Forks account instead said two Black men found hiding in a cornfield on Joseph Webb's farm were questioned by officers and released because there was no evidence to hold them.

No report of the hunted man's capture, of any charge, or of how the search ended was found. The motive was called a mystery; the girl told officers she had seen a strange man with a revolver, a mask and a gag near the house two weeks earlier, and her father suspected two men seen loitering there.

The United Press version ran on August 5 and 6 in papers from Oregon and Washington to Ohio and Virginia, under headlines such as "Vengeful Mob Is Seeking for Negro" in the East Oregonian and "Missouri Mob Pursues Negro" in the Seattle Star. Some editors sharpened it: the Salem Daily Capital Journal headlined a "Negro Assailant of White Girl," and the Richmond Virginian called the man a "Fiend" whom the mob would burn "at the stake."

A second line of coverage, datelined Independence, made no mention of a mob and called the attacker an "unidentified man." The Omaha Bee printed it twice and added that the girl "could not tell the police whether her assailant was a negro," while the Daily Missoulian repeated it as late as August 17 with no reference to race. The Grand Forks Evening Times printed the longest account, built on the girl's own statement to officers.

The accounts differ on whether the attacker was Black: the wire stated it as an accusation, while the Independence dispatches, which carry the girl's own statement, said she did not see him. They also differ on her age, 15 in the wire and 16 at Independence, and on the spelling of her name, "Bladus" or "Baldus."

bases: Wire reports said an armed mob was hunting a Black man accused of attacking a white farmer's daughter and threatened to burn him, but no report says he was caught or harmed (A1, A2, A6).

A mob or posse of about one hundred men hunted a Black man and threatened to burn him for an alleged attack on a girl (A1, A10), but no paper reports that anyone was caught or killed, so the episode is a threatened lynching only.

Wire reports agree that a mob hunted a Black man and threatened to burn him (A1, A2, A6), but the Independence dispatches say the girl could not say whether her attacker was Black and that two Black men questioned were released for lack of evidence (A5, A10).

accounts.gist: She heard footsteps, was seized and gagged, lost consciousness and woke tied to a chair; she did not see the man. Two Black men found in a cornfield were questioned and released, and a posse of one hundred searched.

framing.detail: Western and Midwestern papers ran the United Press item under headlines such as 'Vengeful Mob Is Seeking for Negro' and 'Missouri Mob Pursues Negro,' treating the man's guilt as an accusation.
The Salem and Richmond papers headlined a 'Negro Assailant of White Girl' and a 'Fiend,' stating the accusation as fact in the headline.

The Omaha Bee and Grand Forks Evening Times ran the Independence version, which called the attacker 'unidentified,' noted the girl could not say whether he was a negro and reported that the men questioned were released.

info: Attack on the girl and the manhunt on Friday, Aug. 5, 1910 (wire and Independence dispatches dated Aug. 5).
Baldus farm nine miles east of Independence (the Daniel Mason farm); mob hunting in the brush near Buckner, Mo.

Target of the mob: an unnamed Black man hunted in the brush; a second unnamed Black man taken away by authorities (wire); two unnamed Black men found in a cornfield questioned and released (Grand Forks). Victim of the alleged assault: Clara Baldus (wire also 'Bladus'), 15 or 16, white.
Accused of attacking Clara Baldus, who was seized, gagged, chloroformed and tied to a chair in her home; she said she did not see the attacker and could not say whether he was Black.
An armed 'mob' with guns and clubs (wire); a 'neighborhood posse' of about one hundred men, most from a nearby stone quarry (Grand Forks).
No report of the hunted man's capture or of the mob's end was found; the motive for the attack was called 'a mystery.'
